# Spring Boot Web Application using jlink and Multi-Architecture Image Builds

A working Spring Boot image for one CPU architecture does not establish that its
custom Java runtime will work on another. This example combines two container
image techniques:

- creating a custom Java runtime with `jlink`;
- building a multi-platform OCI archive whose index points to separate
  platform-specific image manifests.

It is intentionally a composition example. You can read and run it on its own,
but it does not repeat the full explanation from the deeper examples:

- [Spring Boot Web Application using Slim Java runtime (JRE)](../jlink-slim-image-spring-boot/README.md)
  explains module selection and the mechanics of building a smaller runtime
  image with `jlink`.
- [Spring Boot Web Application using Multi-Architecture Image Builds](../multi-architecture-image-builds-spring-boot/README.md)
  explains OCI image indexes, platform-specific manifests, and local
  multi-platform archive inspection in more detail.

The interaction between those two ideas is the point of this exercise. A `jlink`
runtime is platform-specific. The Dockerfile runs `jlink` separately for
`linux/amd64` and `linux/arm64`, then the local OCI archive lets you inspect the
resulting image index and its platform descriptors. The index inspection
establishes which variants were packaged; it does not test either variant at
runtime.

This focused example does not cover every aspect of running Java in containers.
It leaves out runtime verification, non-root users, signing, scanning,
observability, SBOMs, and deployment hardening. For a more holistic Spring Boot
container example, see
[all-in-one-spring-boot](../all-in-one-spring-boot/README.md).

## Learning objectives

By the end of this example, attendees can:

- inspect the Dockerfile and identify which artefacts are shared and which are
  built for each target platform;
- build a local OCI archive for `linux/amd64` and `linux/arm64`;
- inspect the index and compare its platform descriptors and manifest digests;
  and
- explain why the same JAR can be copied into both variants while the custom
  Java runtime must be built separately for each.

## Prerequisites

The JDK, a container builder, Skopeo, `jq`, and `tree` are used by the
documented steps. The builder must be running and able to execute both target
architectures. The runbook also checks for `curl`, although no walkthrough
command currently uses it.

- [Oracle Java 25](https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/downloads/#java25)

- Either [Docker](https://docs.docker.com/get-docker/) with Buildx, or
  [Podman](https://podman.io/) with manifest support.

- [Skopeo](https://github.com/containers/skopeo).

- `curl`, used to call the Spring Boot endpoint.

- `jq`, used to inspect OCI JSON documents.

- `tree`, used to inspect generated directories in the walkthrough.

Additional setup inputs:

- The main flow writes an OCI archive locally. It does not push a tag to a
  registry or run either platform variant.

- A container build backend that can execute both `linux/amd64` and
  `linux/arm64` containers. This is required because the Dockerfile runs
  `dnf` and `jlink` while building each platform variant.

  The backend that you choose must be configured to support both platforms.
  For example, a Docker Buildx builder may provide this support directly,
  while a Podman host may need `binfmt` handlers for foreign architectures,
  such as:

  ```shell
  podman run --privileged --rm docker.io/tonistiigi/binfmt --install all
  ```

  Configure the backend that you will use before continuing, regardless of
  the operating system on which it runs.

### Oracle Container Registry access

Before pulling an Oracle Java base image, sign in to Oracle Container Registry
and accept the terms for the
[Oracle Java JDK repository](https://container-registry.oracle.com/ords/ocr/ba/java/jdk).

1. Accept the Oracle Container Registry terms.

2. Authenticate your container engine with your own Oracle Container Registry
   username and authentication token.

   Pass the token through standard input so it is neither recorded in shell
   history nor copied into the project or image layers. If you use Podman, use
   its equivalent `login --password-stdin` command.

   ```shell
   docker login container-registry.oracle.com \
     --username 'ALBERT.ATTARD@ORACLE.COM' \
     --password-stdin < ~/.ocr/auth-token
   ```

   This should print the login succeeded message.

   ```
   Login Succeeded!
   ```

3. Verify that the container engine can pull and run the Oracle Java JDK image.

   ```shell
   docker run --rm 'container-registry.oracle.com/java/jdk:25.0.4.1' java --version
   ```

   Docker pulls the image if necessary, then prints the Java runtime version.

   ```
   java 25.0.4.1 2026-08-18 LTS
   Java(TM) SE Runtime Environment (build 25.0.4.1+1-LTS-5)
   Java HotSpot(TM) 64-Bit Server VM (build 25.0.4.1+1-LTS-5, mixed mode, sharing)
   ```

## The artefacts to inspect

The Spring Boot application is packaged as one executable JAR. Its Java bytecode
is shared input for both image variants. The Dockerfile uses a multi-stage
build: the Oracle JDK builder stage installs `binutils` and runs `jlink` with a
fixed module list; the Oracle Linux final stage copies in the custom runtime and
the JAR. The chosen modules must cover the application’s runtime dependencies;
this example does not derive the list automatically.

During a multi-platform build, the builder stage is evaluated for each target
platform. That means the `RUN jlink` step creates a runtime for the current
target platform variant rather than one shared runtime that is copied into every
image.

```dockerfile
FROM container-registry.oracle.com/java/jdk:25.0.4.1 AS builder

# binutils are needed by the `--strip-debug` command line option.
RUN dnf install -y binutils && dnf clean all

ARG JAVA_MODULES=java.base,java.compiler,java.desktop,java.instrument,java.management,java.naming,java.sql,java.security.jgss
RUN jlink \
      --output "/opt/jre" \
      --no-header-files \
      --no-man-pages \
      --strip-debug \
      --add-modules "${JAVA_MODULES}" \
      --compress=zip-9

FROM container-registry.oracle.com/os/oraclelinux:10-slim
WORKDIR "/opt/app"

COPY --from=builder ["/opt/jre", "/opt/jre"]

ARG JAR_FILE="./target/jlink-multi-architecture-spring-boot-*.jar"
COPY ["${JAR_FILE}", "app.jar"]

EXPOSE 8080

ENTRYPOINT ["/opt/jre/bin/java", "-jar", "app.jar"]
```

The Dockerfile contains no explicit operating-system or architecture
conditionals. Its base-image tags resolve to the requested platform variants,
and each `RUN` instruction executes within that variant. As a result, the same
Dockerfile creates an `amd64` custom runtime for the `linux/amd64` image and an
`arm64` custom runtime for the `linux/arm64` image.

## Build the application

Run the build from this example directory. Maven creates
`target/jlink-multi-architecture-spring-boot-1.0.0.jar`, the controlled input
copied into each platform-specific image variant. The custom Java runtime is
created separately inside each target-platform build.

1. Build the application and confirm that the executable JAR is available to
   the later container build.

   ```shell
   ./mvnw clean package
   ```

   Inspect `target/` for the executable JAR. The `.jar.original`
   file is Maven’s un-repackaged input; the Dockerfile copies the `.jar` file.

   ```shell
   tree --dirsfirst --sort=name -L 1 --prune './target/'
   ```

   Spring Boot creates one executable JAR containing the application classes,
   Spring Boot launcher, and nested dependency JARs.

   ```
   ./target/
   ├── jlink-multi-architecture-spring-boot-1.0.0.jar
   └── jlink-multi-architecture-spring-boot-1.0.0.jar.original

   1 directory, 2 files
   ```

## Guided walkthrough

Run these commands from this example directory. A multi-platform application
image can only target platforms supported by every platform-specific input it
depends on. In this example, both the JDK builder image and the Oracle Linux
final-stage image need variants for the requested platforms. Inspect their raw
indexes before building the archive.

1. Inspect the Oracle Java builder image. Look for `linux/amd64` and
   `linux/arm64` descriptors; both are needed to run `jlink` in the builder
   stage for the requested platforms.

   ```shell
   skopeo inspect --raw 'docker://container-registry.oracle.com/java/jdk:25.0.4.1' | jq
   ```

   Check that the JDK image index lists both linux/amd64 and linux/arm64.

   ```json
   {
     "schemaVersion": 2,
     "mediaType": "application/vnd.docker.distribution.manifest.list.v2+json",
     "manifests": [
       {
         "mediaType": "application/vnd.docker.distribution.manifest.v2+json",
         "size": 1099,
         "digest": "sha256:06d115c14b85dc23030635780c6a587096dfb0583085c31d36be634b7efe49f2",
         "platform": {
           "architecture": "arm64",
           "os": "linux"
         }
       },
       {
         "mediaType": "application/vnd.docker.distribution.manifest.v2+json",
         "size": 1099,
         "digest": "sha256:c2fde8cea2f620b6b7dafc53fa9a4ac3f88ed41ad1ad35e085c56decdfc96d12",
         "platform": {
           "architecture": "amd64",
           "os": "linux"
         }
       }
     ]
   }
   ```

2. Inspect the Oracle Linux final-stage image. It also needs descriptors for
   both platforms so each final image has a matching base.

   ```shell
   skopeo inspect --raw 'docker://container-registry.oracle.com/os/oraclelinux:10-slim' | jq
   ```

   Check that the Oracle Linux image index lists both target platforms.

   ```json
   {
     "schemaVersion": 2,
     "mediaType": "application/vnd.oci.image.index.v1+json",
     "manifests": [
       {
         "mediaType": "application/vnd.docker.distribution.manifest.v2+json",
         "digest": "sha256:fd97561c070364cd3e640b18848f28a3184f0126ec4ab062351c7dab1a147be2",
         "size": 429,
         "platform": {
           "architecture": "amd64",
           "os": "linux"
         }
       },
       {
         "mediaType": "application/vnd.docker.distribution.manifest.v2+json",
         "digest": "sha256:e1fc77b5efd9a7a6af6e2b0912c0d3810ee73715d3168f18064d407bc6308f5f",
         "size": 429,
         "platform": {
           "architecture": "arm64",
           "os": "linux"
         }
       }
     ]
   }
   ```

Both base image tags need `linux/amd64` and `linux/arm64` variants because those
are the two platforms requested later in this runbook.

### Build a multi-platform OCI archive

Docker Buildx and Podman can both produce a multi-platform OCI archive without
pushing to a registry. The important difference from the plain
multi-architecture example is that this Dockerfile runs `jlink` during the
build. The builder must therefore execute the `RUN jlink` step in a way that
produces a valid runtime for each requested target platform.

The runbook executes the Docker route on macOS and the Podman route on Linux.
Both routes are intended to produce an OCI archive at
`./target/jlink-multi-architecture.tar`.

1. Build the multi-platform OCI archive. A successful build creates a local
   archive containing an image index and platform-specific image manifests; it
   does not by itself verify that either image starts correctly.

   The `--platform` option tells the builder which operating system and CPU
   architecture combinations to build for. Here we request two Linux image
   variants: `linux/amd64` for x86-64 machines and `linux/arm64` for 64-bit ARM
   machines.

   - Using Docker.

     ```shell
     docker buildx build \
       --platform 'linux/amd64,linux/arm64' \
       --file './containers/Dockerfile' \
       --tag 'demo:jlink-multi-architecture-oci' \
       --output 'type=oci,dest=./target/jlink-multi-architecture.tar' \
       .
     ```

     The `--output 'type=oci,dest=./target/jlink-multi-architecture.tar'` option
     exports the build result as an OCI image archive instead of loading it
     directly into the local image store. Because this build targets multiple
     platforms, the archive contains an OCI image index together with the
     platform-specific image manifests and layers.

   - Using Podman.

     ```shell
     podman manifest rm 'demo:jlink-multi-architecture-oci' 2>/dev/null || true

     podman build \
       --platform 'linux/amd64,linux/arm64' \
       --security-opt 'label=disable' \
       --file './containers/Dockerfile' \
       --manifest 'demo:jlink-multi-architecture-oci' \
       .

     podman manifest push \
       'demo:jlink-multi-architecture-oci' \
       'oci-archive:./target/jlink-multi-architecture.tar'
     ```

     `--manifest` names the Podman manifest list that collects the `linux/amd64`
     and `linux/arm64` images produced by this build. The subsequent
     `podman manifest push` command exports that manifest list, together with
     its platform-specific images, to the OCI archive.

     `--security-opt 'label=disable'` disables SELinux labelling for the
     temporary build containers. This allows the QEMU interpreter registered
     through `binfmt` to execute the foreign-architecture build steps on hosts
     where the default Podman SELinux label prevents it. It does not change the
     SELinux labelling of containers created from the resulting image.

   (*Optional*) Verify that the file was created.

   ```shell
   tree --dirsfirst --sort=name --prune -P '*.tar' './target'
   ```

   The OCI image archive should now be present under `target`.

   ```
   ./target
   └── jlink-multi-architecture.tar

   1 directory, 1 file
   ```

2. Inspect the OCI image index stored in the archive. Check that the nested
   index lists both requested Linux platforms.

   ```shell
   IMAGE_INDEX_DIGEST="$(
     tar --extract --to-stdout --file './target/jlink-multi-architecture.tar' 'index.json' \
       | jq --raw-output '.manifests[0].digest | sub("^sha256:"; "")'
   )"

   tar --extract --to-stdout --file './target/jlink-multi-architecture.tar' "blobs/sha256/${IMAGE_INDEX_DIGEST}" | jq
   ```

   The nested OCI index lists separate manifests for the requested platforms.

   ```json
   {
     "schemaVersion": 2,
     "mediaType": "application/vnd.oci.image.index.v1+json",
     "manifests": [
       {
         "mediaType": "application/vnd.oci.image.manifest.v1+json",
         "digest": "sha256:f339aa2ba60528d1a46fe52f39baf4f66912515ce874edb1a0505bb87dc40bd7",
         "size": 1014,
         "platform": {
           "architecture": "arm64",
           "os": "linux"
         }
       },
       {
         "mediaType": "application/vnd.oci.image.manifest.v1+json",
         "digest": "sha256:9e61628acada9ba896202b99959c9b0dc25b56e395780fe41320c18e7dfe7757",
         "size": 1014,
         "platform": {
           "architecture": "amd64",
           "os": "linux"
         }
       }
     ]
   }
   ```

   The archive’s image index contains one descriptor for each requested
   platform. Each descriptor points to a separate image manifest, and each image
   manifest references the layers for that platform’s final image. Because
   `jlink` ran during the build, the custom runtime copied into the final image
   is part of the platform-specific result.

3. Re-read the same image index and compare the platform-specific manifest
   digests. This command repeats step 2; it does not open the referenced
   manifests or prove that their Java runtimes execute successfully.

   ```shell
   IMAGE_INDEX_DIGEST="$(
     tar --extract --to-stdout --file './target/jlink-multi-architecture.tar' 'index.json' \
       | jq --raw-output '.manifests[0].digest | sub("^sha256:"; "")'
   )"

   tar --extract --to-stdout --file './target/jlink-multi-architecture.tar' "blobs/sha256/${IMAGE_INDEX_DIGEST}" | jq
   ```

   Re-reading the same index exposes the digest paired with each platform.

   ```json
   {
     "schemaVersion": 2,
     "mediaType": "application/vnd.oci.image.index.v1+json",
     "manifests": [
       {
         "mediaType": "application/vnd.oci.image.manifest.v1+json",
         "digest": "sha256:f339aa2ba60528d1a46fe52f39baf4f66912515ce874edb1a0505bb87dc40bd7",
         "size": 1014,
         "platform": {
           "architecture": "arm64",
           "os": "linux"
         }
       },
       {
         "mediaType": "application/vnd.oci.image.manifest.v1+json",
         "digest": "sha256:9e61628acada9ba896202b99959c9b0dc25b56e395780fe41320c18e7dfe7757",
         "size": 1014,
         "platform": {
           "architecture": "amd64",
           "os": "linux"
         }
       }
     ]
   }
   ```

   Different manifest digests indicate that the index refers to separate image
   manifests for the requested platforms. The descriptors do not show layer
   contents or prove runtime compatibility. The Dockerfile and build stages
   establish the intended platform-specific `jlink` work; running both variants
   would be a separate verification step.

## Key takeaways and trade-offs

- The OCI index makes the two target platforms and their distinct image manifest
  digests visible under one image result.
- One executable JAR can be shared, while `jlink` must create a runtime in each
  platform’s builder stage.
- A multi-platform build requires matching base-image variants and a builder
  capable of executing both platforms, which may need additional host setup.
- Archive inspection verifies packaging metadata, not startup behaviour or
  production suitability; test each variant in its intended environment.
